The story contains several emotional and behavioral turns that are unexpected yet deeply fitting for the characters. First, when the narrator returns after the mother's heatstroke, it is surprising to discover that the pragmatic, unsentimental mother has preserved the "remnants" of the narrator's previous visit—washing the mug but placing it right back on the counter where it was left, turning the family photo toward the door, and rationing the blackberry jam one spoonful a day. While unexpected given her stoic exterior, this turn is completely appropriate because it aligns with how she has always expressed love: through quiet rituals, household objects, and practical habits rather than open emotion. 

Second, at the end of the story, the narrator makes the surprising choice to break a twenty-year habit of washing the dishes before leaving, intentionally leaving the glasses, knife, and plate in the sink. In hindsight, this is entirely appropriate because the narrator has just realized that these leftover items are what keep the visit "alive" for the lonely mother after the narrator is gone. Leaving the dishes is an unspoken gift, giving the mother new remnants to hold onto.
